title: A Dominican day at home

lines: COULD A HOME DAY HAVE THEIR SHAPE?
cards: No friary. No white habit. No bell in a cloister calling anyone to choir.
Just a kitchen, a phone on the counter, a commute, a shift, dinner, and dishes.

For these last weeks this path has followed the Dominicans: an innkeeper up all night, nuns before friars, a motto of truth, a climber in Turin, a theologian who waited, a painter's quiet walls, a founder's last promise.
Today is the last day with them, and it asks a small question. Could an ordinary day, in an ordinary house, have the Dominican shape?

teach.b: Here's the shape, in three motions. Morning: pray. It can be short.

A Dominican at home might pray one psalm before the phone comes on. A psalm in the Douay-Rheims gives a line that fits: "O Lord, in the morning thou shalt hear my voice." Morning first, before the day gets its say.
Midday: study. One page, chewed slowly: a Gospel passage, a paragraph of the catechism, a few lines of a saint.
For the friars in the university towns, study wasn't a hobby beside prayer; it was prayer with the mind switched on.
Evening: share one truth. Not a lecture. One true thing you learned or noticed today, handed to someone: at dinner, in a text, while folding laundry.
That's the preacher in the house.
Thomas Aquinas, the Dominican teacher, has a phrase for the whole pattern that Dominicans still quote: contemplata aliis tradere, to contemplate, and to hand on to others what you've contemplated.

teach.h: IN THE MORNING THOU SHALT HEAR MY VOICE.
teach.b: Prayer and study fill the cup. Sharing pours it out. If one of the three goes missing, the day tips: all prayer and no sharing turns inward, all sharing and no study runs dry.
Tomorrow a new family arrives, the Jesuits, with a book of their own in hand.

how: Lay Dominicans and others drawn to the order shape ordinary days around prayer, study and sharing, some praying morning and evening prayer from the Liturgy of the Hours and reading scripture or a spiritual book each day.

games.q: it's evening. you prayed this morning and read one page at lunch. what's left of the Dominican day?
o: share one true thing you learned with someone.
games.why: the third motion is sharing: contemplate, then hand on to others what you've contemplated.

practice: Think back over these days with the Dominicans and find one thing that stuck: a story, a phrase, a picture. Say it to yourself in one plain sentence, as if explaining it to a friend who's never heard of Dominic.
If you pray, ask that it reach someone as a gift, not a sermon.

wordCard.voice: A Dominican day at home. Pray in the morning, study at midday, share one true thing at night: the order's rhythm, fitted around an ordinary life. Today's word.

orig.note: Latin, from Thomas Aquinas: to hand on to others what has been contemplated.

carryVoice: Your line: pray, study, share. That's the Dominican stretch, folded into one ordinary day. See you tomorrow.
